Section 2.1 of Lock⁵ turns to **categorical variables**. The raw information in a
categorical variable is summarized with a **frequency table** (counts), converted
to shares with a **relative frequency table**, and visualized with a **bar chart**.
The workhorse statistic is a **proportion** — the fraction of cases falling in a
category of interest — written $\hat p$ for a sample and $p$ for a population.
Two categorical variables are summarized together in a **two-way table**, from
which we read **marginal** percentages (computed out of everyone) and
**conditional** percentages (computed within a row or column), and we compare
groups with a **difference in proportions**. The exercises below are from
*Statistics: Unlocking the Power of Data* (Lock⁵, 3rd ed., pp. 61–71):
Skill Builders 2.1–2.12 practice finding proportions with correct notation,
building relative frequency tables, and reading two-way tables; 2.13–2.31 apply
the ideas to real studies; 2.32–2.35 use the ACHA–NCHA college survey;
2.36–2.38 analyze a smoking-cessation experiment; 2.39–2.53 investigate
association in two-way tables, with several technology exercises on Lock5 data
files. Tabs based on Lock5 data files include a small executable EDA.

## Exercise 2.1

The survey students consisted of 169 females and 193 males. Find $\hat p$, the
proportion who are female.

- $\hat p = \dfrac{169}{169+193} = \dfrac{169}{362} \approx 0.467$. About 46.7%
  of the survey students are female.

## Exercise 2.2

The survey included 43 students who smoke and 319 who don't. Find $\hat p$, the
proportion who smoke.

- $\hat p = \dfrac{43}{43+319} = \dfrac{43}{362} \approx 0.119$. About 11.9% of
  the survey students smoke.

## Exercise 2.3

Of the students who identified their class year, 94 were first years, 195 were
sophomores, 35 were juniors, and 36 were seniors. Find $\hat p$, the proportion
who are upperclass students (juniors or seniors).

- $\hat p = \dfrac{35+36}{94+195+35+36} = \dfrac{71}{360} \approx 0.197$. About
  19.7% are upperclass students.

## Exercise 2.4

The math SAT score is higher than the verbal SAT score for 205 of the 355
students who answered the questions about SAT scores. Find $\hat p$, the
proportion for whom the math SAT score is higher.

- $\hat p = \dfrac{205}{355} \approx 0.577$. About 57.7% of the respondents did
  better on the math SAT than on the verbal SAT.

## Exercise 2.5

In the 2010 US Census, we see that 37,342,870 people, or 12.4% of all residents,
are foreign-born. Give the relevant proportion using correct notation.

- $p = 0.124$ — a **population proportion**, since the Census includes (essentially)
  all US residents. It is the proportion of all US residents who are foreign-born.

## Exercise 2.6

A recent headline states that 45% think children of illegal immigrants should be
able to attend public school. The report gives the results of a survey of 1000
randomly selected likely voters in the US. Give the relevant proportion using
correct notation.

- $\hat p = 0.45$ — a **sample proportion**, based on a random sample of 1000
  likely voters. It is the proportion of the sampled voters who think children
  of illegal immigrants should be able to attend public school.

## Exercise 2.7

A survey conducted of 1060 randomly selected US teens aged 13 to 17 found that
605 of them say they have made a new friend online. Give the relevant proportion
using correct notation.

- $\hat p = \dfrac{605}{1060} \approx 0.571$ — a sample proportion: the proportion
  of the sampled US teens who say they have made a new friend online.

## Exercise 2.8

Of all 2,220,087 members of the high school class of 2019 who took the SAT,
554,665 reported their race as Hispanic/Latino. Give the relevant proportion
using correct notation.

- $p = \dfrac{554{,}665}{2{,}220{,}087} \approx 0.250$ — a **population
  proportion**, since the data include every member of the class who took the
  SAT: the proportion of all SAT takers in the class of 2019 who reported their

## Exercise 2.9

Of the 362 students who answered the question about what award they would
prefer, 31 preferred an Academy Award, 149 preferred a Nobel Prize, and 182
preferred an Olympic gold medal. Construct a relative frequency table of the
data, rounded to three decimal places.

```{python}
#| echo: false
award = pd.DataFrame(
    {"Frequency": [31, 149, 182]},
    index=["Academy Award", "Nobel Prize", "Olympic gold medal"])
award["Rel. Freq."] = (award["Frequency"] / award["Frequency"].sum()).round(3)
award
```

- The relative frequencies are 0.086 (Academy Award), 0.412 (Nobel Prize), and
  0.503 (Olympic gold medal). They sum to 1.001 rather than 1 only because of
  rounding.

## Exercise 2.10

Of the 361 students who answered the question about the number of piercings,
188 had no piercings, 82 had one or two piercings, and the rest had more than
two. Construct a relative frequency table, rounded to three decimal places.

```{python}
#| echo: false
piercings = pd.DataFrame(
    {"Frequency": [188, 82, 361 - 188 - 82]},
    index=["No piercings", "One or two", "More than two"])
piercings["Rel. Freq."] = (piercings["Frequency"] / 361).round(3)
piercings
```

- The relative frequencies are 0.521 (no piercings), 0.227 (one or two), and
  0.252 (more than two), which sum to 1.

## Exercise 2.11

A two-way table for two groups and two outcomes:

```{python}
#| echo: false
tw = pd.DataFrame({"Outcome A": [20, 60], "Outcome B": [80, 40]},
                  index=["Group 1", "Group 2"])
tw["Total"] = tw.sum(axis=1)
tw.loc["Total"] = tw.sum()
tw
```

- **(a)** Proportion of all cases with Outcome A: $\dfrac{80}{200} = 0.40$.
- **(b)** Proportion of all cases in Group 1: $\dfrac{100}{200} = 0.50$.
- **(c)** Proportion of cases in Group 1 with Outcome B:
  $\dfrac{80}{100} = 0.80$.
- **(d)** Proportion of cases with Outcome A that were in Group 2:
  $\dfrac{60}{80} = 0.75$.

## Exercise 2.15

Home Field Advantage in Soccer: across 43 professional soccer leagues in 24
different countries, covering more than 66,000 games, the home field advantage
(percent of games won by the home team) is 62.4%. Is this a population or a
sample? What are the cases and approximately how many are there? What is the
variable and is it categorical or quantitative? What is the relevant statistic,
including correct notation?

- **Population** — the dataset covers *all* games played in those 43 leagues,
  not a sample of them.
- **Cases:** individual games — more than 66,000 of them.
- **Variable:** whether the home team won the game — **categorical** (win/loss,
  ignoring ties or treating each game's result as the outcome of interest).
- **Relevant statistic (parameter):** the population proportion of games won by
  the home team, $p = 0.624$.

## Exercise 2.16

What Proportion of College Students Have a Paying Job? The 2018 Your First
College Year survey included 5204 first-year, full-time college students:
1436 work on campus, 1119 work off campus, and 2649 do not work.

```{python}
#| echo: false
job = pd.DataFrame(
    {"Frequency": [1436, 1119, 2649]},
    index=["Works on campus", "Works off campus", "Does not work"])
job["Rel. Freq."] = (job["Frequency"] / 5204).round(3)
job
```

- **(a)** Proportion who do not work at a paying job:
  $\dfrac{2649}{5204} \approx 0.509$.
- **(b)** Proportion who do work at a paying job (on or off campus):
  $\dfrac{1436+1119}{5204} = \dfrac{2555}{5204} \approx 0.491$.
- **(c)** The relative frequency table above: 0.276 on campus, 0.215 off
  campus, 0.509 not working.

## Exercise 2.17

Which Food Delivery App Is Most Popular? Among US smartphone users who regularly
use a food delivery app, the proportions using each app most recently are:

```{python}
#| echo: false
apps = pd.DataFrame(
    {"Proportion": [0.276, 0.267, 0.252, 0.121, np.nan]},
    index=["DoorDash", "Grubhub", "UberEats", "Postmates", "Other"])
apps.loc["Other", "Proportion"] = 1 - apps["Proportion"].sum()
apps.round(3)
```

- **(a)** A **relative frequency table** — the entries are proportions of the
  sample of food delivery app users, not counts and not a two-way table.
- **(b)** The missing value: $1 - (0.276+0.267+0.252+0.121) = 0.084$. About
  8.4% of users in the sample selected some other app.

## Exercise 2.18

Airborne Antibiotics: scientists analyzed 20 samples of dust particles from
animal farms; tylosin, an antibiotic used in animal feed, showed up in 16 of
the samples.

- **(a) Variable:** whether the antibiotic tylosin is present in the dust sample
  (**categorical**). **Cases:** the 20 dust samples.
- **(b)** Frequency table below.
- **(c)** Bar chart below.
- **(d)** Relative frequency table: $\dfrac{16}{20} = 0.80$ of the samples
  contain tylosin, $\dfrac{4}{20} = 0.20$ do not.

```{python}
#| echo: false

tylo
```

```{python}
#| echo: false
```

## Exercise 2.19

Rock-Paper-Scissors: a study observed 119 people playing the game. Their
choices are shown below.

```{python}
#| echo: false
rps = pd.DataFrame(
    {"Frequency": [66, 39, 14]},
    index=["Rock", "Paper", "Scissors"])
rps["Rel. Freq."] = (rps["Frequency"] / 119).round(3)
rps
```

- **(a) Sample:** the 119 people observed playing the game. **Population:**
  all people who play Rock-Paper-Scissors (broadly, people in situations where
  the game is used). **Variable:** which option the player throws — rock, paper,
  or scissors (**categorical**).
- **(b)** Relative frequency table above: 0.555 rock, 0.328 paper, 0.118
  scissors.
- **(c)** Play **paper**. Opponents throw rock far more often than anything
  else (about 56% of the time), so paper — which beats rock — wins most often.
- **(d)** Play **scissors**. Players tend to repeat the option they just threw,
  so an opponent who just played paper is likely to play paper again — and
  scissors beats paper.

## Exercise 2.20

Sports-Related Concussions in Kids: all sports-related concussions reported to
an emergency room for children ages 5 to 18 in the US over one year, by activity:

```{python}
#| echo: false
conc = pd.DataFrame(
    {"Frequency": [23405, 20293, 11507, 10414, 7667, 7433,
                   5220, 4408, 4111, 3846, 2648]},
    index=["Bicycles", "Football", "Basketball", "Playground", "Soccer",
           "Baseball", "All-Terrain Vehicle", "Skateboarding", "Hockey",
           "Swimming", "Horseback Riding"])
conc["Proportion"] = (conc["Frequency"] / conc["Frequency"].sum()).round(3)
conc
```

- **(a)** These results come from a **population**: every concussion reported
  to emergency rooms for this age group over the year was included.
- **(b)** Proportion from football:
  $\dfrac{20{,}293}{100{,}952} \approx 0.201$ (about 20.1%).
- **(c)** Proportion from bicycles:
  $\dfrac{23{,}405}{100{,}952} \approx 0.232$ (about 23.2%).
- **(d) No.** These proportions only tell us how the *concussions* are
  distributed across activities — not how dangerous each activity is. Many more
  children ride bicycles than play football, so per hour of participation,
  football could still be riskier. Without knowing how many children take part
  in each activity (the exposure), we cannot compare the danger of the
  activities themselves.

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: Sports-related concussions in children ages 5 to 18 by activity
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.5, 4))
conc["Frequency"].sort_values().plot.barh(ax=ax, color="#4c72b0")
ax.set_xlabel("Number of concussions")
ax.set_ylabel("")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

## Exercise 2.21

Does Belief in One True Love Differ by Education Level? Two-way table of
agreement with the statement that there is only one true love, by education
level (HS = high school or less, Some = some college, College = college
graduate or higher):

```{python}
#| echo: false
love = pd.DataFrame(
    {"HS": [363, 557, 20], "Some": [176, 466, 26], "College": [196, 789, 32]},
    index=["Agree", "Disagree", "Don't know"])
love["Total"] = love.sum(axis=1)
love.loc["Total"] = love.sum()
love
```

- **(a)** The table above includes row and column totals (2625 participants).
- **(b)** Percent agreeing, within each education level: HS
  $\dfrac{363}{940} \approx 38.6\%$; Some college
  $\dfrac{176}{668} \approx 26.3\%$; College
  $\dfrac{196}{1017} \approx 19.3\%$. **Yes, there is an association** —
  agreement with one true love *decreases* as education increases.
- **(c)** Percent with a college degree or higher:
  $\dfrac{1017}{2625} \approx 38.7\%$.
- **(d)** Of those who disagree, percent with a high school degree or less:
  $\dfrac{557}{1812} \approx 30.7\%$.

## Exercise 2.22

Juvenile Diabetes Treatment: 76 children at high risk for Type 1 diabetes were
randomly assigned to the drug teplizumab or a control group; 42 developed the
disease during the study.

```{python}
#| echo: false
diab = pd.DataFrame({"Diabetes": [16, 26], "No diabetes": [22, 12]},
                    index=["Teplizumab", "Control"])
diab["Total"] = diab.sum(axis=1)
diab.loc["Total"] = diab.sum()
diab
```

- **(a)** Control group: $\hat p_C = \dfrac{26}{38} \approx 0.684$.
- **(b)** Teplizumab group: $\hat p_T = \dfrac{16}{38} \approx 0.421$.
- **(c)** Difference in proportions:
  $\hat p_C - \hat p_T = 0.684 - 0.421 \approx 0.263$.
- **(d)** An **experiment** — participants were randomly assigned to the two
  treatments.
- **(e) Yes.** Because the drug was randomly assigned, confounding variables are
  balanced between the groups, so a strong difference in proportions supports
  the conclusion that teplizumab is responsible for stopping and/or delaying
  the onset of the disease.

## Exercise 2.23

Social Media Use and ADHD: teens aged 15–16 without ADHD symptoms were rated
for frequency of digital social media use and followed for two years.

```{python}
#| echo: false
adhd = pd.DataFrame({"ADHD": [16, 23], "No ADHD": [149, 472]},
                    index=["High frequency", "Low frequency"])
adhd["Total"] = adhd.sum(axis=1)
adhd.loc["Total"] = adhd.sum()
adhd
```

- **(a)** $\hat p_1 = \dfrac{16}{165} \approx 0.097$ (high frequency users).
- **(b)** $\hat p_2 = \dfrac{23}{495} \approx 0.046$ (low frequency users).
- **(c)** The **high frequency** group had a higher proportion developing ADHD
  symptoms (about 9.7% vs 4.6%).
- **(d)** $\hat p_1 - \hat p_2 \approx 0.097 - 0.046 = 0.051$.
- **(e)** Proportion of all teens developing ADHD:
  $\dfrac{39}{660} \approx 0.059$.
- **(f)** An **observational study** — the researchers only *rated* existing
  social media habits; use frequency was not assigned.
- **(g) No.** Without random assignment, confounding variables (personality,
  home environment, sleep, ...) could account for the difference; the study
  shows an association, not a causal effect.

## Exercise 2.24

Playing Hide-and-Seek with Rats: number of times rats entered transparent vs
opaque boxes while hiding or seeking:

```{python}
#| echo: false
rats = pd.DataFrame({"Transparent": [15, 17], "Opaque": [38, 14]},
                    index=["Hiding", "Seeking"])
rats["Total"] = rats.sum(axis=1)
rats.loc["Total"] = rats.sum()
rats
```

- **(a)** When hiding, proportion entering opaque boxes:
  $\hat p_H = \dfrac{38}{53} \approx 0.717$.
- **(b)** When seeking, proportion entering opaque boxes:
  $\hat p_S = \dfrac{14}{31} \approx 0.452$.
- **(c)** Difference: $\hat p_H - \hat p_S \approx 0.717 - 0.452 = 0.265$. The
  notation is $\hat p_H - \hat p_S$, the sample proportion entering opaque boxes
  when hiding minus the sample proportion entering opaque boxes when seeking.
  Rats clearly prefer opaque boxes when they don't want to be seen.

## Exercise 2.25

Antibiotics in Infancy and Weight: 616 children classified by antibiotic
exposure in the first year of life and overweight status at age 9:

```{python}
#| echo: false
abx = pd.DataFrame(
    {"Not overweight": [144, 37], "Overweight": [294, 141]},
    index=["Antibiotics", "No antibiotics"])
abx["Total"] = abx.sum(axis=1)
abx.loc["Total"] = abx.sum()
abx
```

- **(a)** Given antibiotics: $\dfrac{438}{616} \approx 0.711$.
- **(b)** Overweight at age 9: $\dfrac{435}{616} \approx 0.706$.
- **(c)** Overweight among those given antibiotics:
  $\hat p_A = \dfrac{294}{438} \approx 0.671$.
- **(d)** Overweight among those not given antibiotics:
  $\hat p_N = \dfrac{141}{178} \approx 0.792$.
- **(e)** $\hat p_A - \hat p_N \approx 0.671 - 0.792 = -0.121$. Surprisingly,
  children given antibiotics were *less* likely to be overweight in this table.
- **(f)** Of all overweight children, proportion given antibiotics:
  $\dfrac{294}{435} \approx 0.676$.

## Exercise 2.26

Culture and Mental Illness: 60 people with schizophrenia who hear voices (20
each from the US, India, and Ghana), by whether the voices are mostly negative,
neutral, or positive:

```{python}
#| echo: false
voices = pd.DataFrame(
    {"US": [14, 6, 0], "India": [4, 3, 13], "Ghana": [2, 2, 16]},
    index=["Negative", "Neutral", "Positive"])
voices["Total"] = voices.sum(axis=1)
voices.loc["Total"] = voices.sum()
voices
```

- **(a)** Proportion hearing mostly negative voices:
  $\dfrac{20}{60} = \dfrac{1}{3} \approx 0.333$.
- **(b)** US participants: $\dfrac{14}{20} = 0.70$.
- **(c)** Non-US participants: $\dfrac{6}{40} = 0.15$.
- **(d)** Of those hearing positive voices, proportion from the US:
  $\dfrac{0}{29} = 0$ — not a single US participant described the voices as
  mostly positive.
- **(e) Yes** — a strong association: negative voices are the norm for US
  participants (70%) but rare elsewhere (15%), while positive voices are
  reported only outside the US. Culture appears to shape how the voices are
  experienced.

## Exercise 2.27

Does It Pay to Get a College Degree? In 2010, the unemployment rate for high
school graduates with no college degree was 9.7%, while for college graduates
with a bachelor's degree it was only 5.2%. Find the difference in proportions
unemployed between these two groups, with correct notation. The data come from
the census, so treat the values as population proportions, with subscripts
identifying the two groups.

- $p_{HS} - p_{C} = 0.097 - 0.052 = 0.045$. Since these values come from a
  census, we use population proportions $p_{HS}$ (high school graduates with no

  unemployment rate for high school graduates is 4.5 percentage points higher.

- **(a) Variables:** the type of sample (breath or stool — **categorical**) and

- **(b)** Two-way table below.
- **(c)** Breath samples: $\dfrac{33}{36} \approx 0.917$ correct. Stool samples:

- **(d)** Of all correct tests, proportion that were stool tests:

## Exercise 2.29

Is There a Genetic Marker for Dyslexia? A disruption of a gene called DYXC1 on
chromosome 15 may be related to dyslexia. Researchers studied the gene in 109
people diagnosed with dyslexia and a control group of 195 others with no
learning disorder. The DYXC1 break occurred in 10 of those with dyslexia and in
5 of the control group.

- **(a)** An **observational study** — the researchers compared existing groups;
  nobody was assigned to dyslexia or to a gene disruption. **Variables:** group
  (dyslexia vs control — **categorical**) and whether the DYXC1 break occurs
  (yes/no — **categorical**).
- **(b)** **304 rows** (109 + 195 cases) and **2 columns** (the two variables).
- **(c)** Two-way table below.
- **(d)** Dyslexia group: $\dfrac{10}{109} \approx 0.092$ with the break.
  Control group: $\dfrac{5}{195} \approx 0.026$ with the break.
- **(e) Yes** — the marker is more than three times as common in the dyslexia
  group (9.2% vs 2.6%), so there appears to be an association between the
  DYXC1 break and dyslexia in this sample.
- **(f) No.** This is an observational study, so we cannot assume the gene
  disruption *causes* dyslexia — confounding variables are not ruled out.
  (Chapter 4 addresses whether the association generalizes to the population.)

```{python}
#| echo: false
dys = pd.DataFrame({"Break": [10, 5], "No break": [99, 190]},
                   index=["Dyslexia", "Control"])
dys["Total"] = dys.sum(axis=1)
dys.loc["Total"] = dys.sum()
dys
```

## Exercise 2.30

Help for Insomniacs: forty people diagnosed with insomnia were randomly divided
into two groups of 20; one group received a one-hour cognitive behavioral
therapy (CBT) session, the other no treatment. Three months later, 14 of the
therapy group reported sleep improvements versus 3 of the others.

- **(a)** Two-way table below.
- **(b)** $14 + 3 = 17$ of the 40 people reported sleep improvement.
- **(c)** Therapy group: $\hat p_T = \dfrac{14}{20} = 0.70$.
- **(d)** No-treatment group: $\hat p_N = \dfrac{3}{20} = 0.15$.
- **(e)** $\hat p_T - \hat p_N = 0.70 - 0.15 = 0.55$. A single CBT session goes
  with a 55 percentage-point higher rate of reported sleep improvement.

```{python}
#| echo: false
ins = pd.DataFrame({"Improved": [14, 3], "Not improved": [6, 17]},
                   index=["Therapy", "No treatment"])
ins["Total"] = ins.sum(axis=1)
ins.loc["Total"] = ins.sum()
ins
```

## Exercise 2.31

Electrical Stimulation for Fresh Insight? Forty participants were trained to
solve problems one way and then asked to solve an unfamiliar problem requiring
fresh insight; half were randomly assigned to receive non-invasive electrical
brain stimulation and half received sham stimulation as a placebo. Participants
did not know which group they were in. In the control group 20% solved the
problem, while 60% of the stimulation group did.

- **(a)** An **experiment** — the explanatory variable (stimulation vs sham) was
  actively imposed and randomly assigned by the researchers.
- **(b)** **Single-blind** — the participants do not know which group they are
  in. (With sham stimulation the participants are blinded; nothing indicates
  the people measuring the outcome were also unaware.)
- **(c)** **Variables:** treatment received (electrical vs sham stimulation —
  **categorical**) and whether the participant solved the problem (yes/no —
  **categorical**).
- **(d)** Two-way table below.
- **(e)** Of those who solved the problem, percent with electrical stimulation:
  $\dfrac{12}{16} = 75\%$.
- **(f)** $\hat p_E = 0.60$, $\hat p_S = 0.20$, so
  $\hat p_E - \hat p_S = 0.60 - 0.20 = 0.40$.
- **(g) Yes** — the stimulation group was three times as likely to solve the
  problem, and since the study is a randomized (single-blind) experiment, the
  difference is plausibly due to the stimulation itself.

```{python}
#| echo: false
stim = pd.DataFrame({"Solved": [12, 4], "Not solved": [8, 16]},
                    index=["Electrical", "Sham"])
stim["Total"] = stim.sum(axis=1)
stim.loc["Total"] = stim.sum()
stim
```

## Exercise 2.32

Emotionally Abusive Relationships (ACHA–NCHA survey, Table 2.16):

## Exercise 2.34

How Accurate Are Student Perceptions? Students answered both how many drinks
*they* had the last time they partied (Figure 2.3(a)) and how many drinks they
think the *typical student* at their school had (Figure 2.3(b)), shown as
side-by-side bar charts for males and females.

- **(a)** For personal use, the most likely response for both males and females
  is **0 drinks** — the tallest bars in (a) are at zero.
- **(b)** For the typical student, the most likely response for both sexes is
  much higher — around **3–4 drinks**.
- **(c) No.** Students' perceptions of typical alcohol use far exceed reality:
  most students themselves drink nothing, yet they believe the typical student
  drinks several. Students overestimate the norm, plausibly because heavy
  drinkers are the most visible (the same failure to sample representatively
  seen in Chapter 1).

## Exercise 2.35

Does Stress Affect Academic Performance? Students were asked whether stress has
negatively affected their academics. Figure 2.4(a) shows a segmented bar chart
of response *frequencies*; Figure 2.4(b) shows response *relative frequencies*
as percents (red = no stress, green = stress but no effect on grades,
blue = stress hurt grades).

- **(a)** **More females** participated — the female bar in graph (a) is about
  twice the height of the male bar. Only the **frequency** graph (a) can answer
  this.
- **(b)** A **greater number of females** said they had no stress — again read
  from the frequency graph **(a)**.
- **(c)** **Approximately equal** percents of males and females said they had
  no stress — visible only in the relative frequency graph **(b)**.
- **(d)** A greater **percent of females** say stress hurt their grades —
  visible only in the relative frequency graph **(b)**. Parts (a)–(b) and
  (c)–(d) illustrate why frequencies answer how many while relative
  frequencies answer how likely.

## Exercise 2.37

Agreeing to Participate: random assignment put 1017 smokers in the Reward
group, of whom 914 agreed to participate, and 1053 smokers in the Deposit
group, of whom only 146 agreed (they had to risk their own money).

```{python}
                    index=["Reward", "Deposit"])

part
```

- Participation rates: Reward $\dfrac{914}{1017} \approx 0.899$ (89.9%);

  Deposit group agreed to participate.

## Exercise 2.38

Accounting for Participation Rates: among smokers who declined to participate,
30 of those originally in the Deposit group stopped smoking on their own, and
only 3 of the Reward decliners stopped. Compare the proportion of all subjects
originally assigned to each group who quit for six months. (A no-incentive
group at the company had about a 6.0% success rate.)

- **Reward:** $\dfrac{156+3}{1017} = \dfrac{159}{1017} \approx 0.156$ (15.6%).
- **Deposit:** $\dfrac{78+30}{1053} = \dfrac{108}{1053} \approx 0.103$ (10.3%).
- Once non-participants are included, the picture **reverses**: Reward (15.6%)
  beats Deposit (10.3%) for the originally assigned groups, although both still
  beat the 6.0% rate with no incentive. The deposit program looked better in
  Exercise 2.36 only among the self-selected participants — a vivid reminder
  that ignoring non-response can flip a conclusion.

## Exercise 2.40

Association or No Association? An experiment will randomly divide 40 cases
between treatments A and B (20 each) and record Successful / Not successful.
Fill in a two-way table with possible values showing:

- **(a) A clear association**, for example — the success rate differs sharply
  by treatment: Treatment A: 16 successful, 4 not; Treatment B: 8 successful,
  12 not. Then $\hat p_A = 0.80$ versus $\hat p_B = 0.40$.
- **(b) No association at all**, for example — identical success rates:
  Treatment A: 10 successful, 10 not; Treatment B: 10 successful, 10 not. Then
  $\hat p_A = \hat p_B = 0.50$, so treatment and outcome are unrelated.
  (Many other fill-ins are possible; the requirement is merely that the
  margins match the outline: 20 per treatment, 40 total.)

## Exercise 2.46

Credit Card by Server: the Credit variable in RestaurantTips records whether
each bill was paid with a credit card (y) or cash (n). Produce a two-way table
showing the credit/cash distribution for each server, and comment.

```{python}
#| echo: false
sv_credit = pd.crosstab(rt["Server"], rt["Credit"])[["n", "y"]]
sv_credit.index.name = "Server"
pct = pd.crosstab(rt["Server"], rt["Credit"], normalize="index")[["n", "y"]] * 100
pd.concat([sv_credit, pct.round(1).add_suffix(" %")], axis=1)
```

- Servers differ noticeably in how their bills are paid: server **C**'s tables
  pay by credit card almost half the time (46.9%), while server **B**'s pay by
  credit only 23.1% of the time (server A: 35.0%). Cash dominates for A and B,
  while C's split is nearly even.

## Exercise 2.53

Which of These Things Is Not Like the Other? Four students graphed the same
two-way table (college accept/reject decision by type of high school: public,
private, parochial) four ways; Figure 2.5 shows the results. Three graphs come
from the same data, but one is inconsistent with the other three.

- **Graph (b) is the bogus one.** Graphs (a), (c), and (d) are consistent
  views of a single two-way table: the school totals in the grouped bar chart
  (a) match the group totals implied by the side-by-side charts (c) and (d),
  just rearranged. In graph (b) the segments within the Accept and Reject bars
  do not add up to the school totals implied by the other three panels — the
  heights disagree with the margins of the same table — so (b) cannot have been
  drawn from these data. The lesson: when several graphs claim to show one
  dataset, check that the margins (totals) agree across all of them.

:::
